Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
Greetings all.
In response to recent debate about broken cards, I am posting a list of
cards I think are broken, or overpowered in some way, along with some
suggested fixes.

Card Suggested Fix
-----------------------------
Day Operation Allies may still block
Zip Gun Cannot use ammo
Tomb of Rameses III You may not transfer off the vampire with ToR
Pulled Fangs (etc.) Rule that it takes 2 ag to burn a vamp at 0 blood
Thoughts Betrayed Not usable against older vamp
Majesty (etc.) S:CE now means "S:Round Ends"- one may still press
Return to Innocence Requires vamp at capacity
-----------------------------
Please suggest other cards to add, or alternate fixes. I'm not sure Mind
Rape and Kiss of Ra are busted, and need some more convincing. I suspect
that RTI is the main reason Mind Rape is so powerful. Otherwise, it is
hard to burn one's own vampires.

In suggesting fixes, I have attempted to follow the following rules.

1) -- Fixes should be brief, using few words. If the fix is significantly
longer and harder to remember than "This card is banned", then I feel that
banning the card would be a better solution.

2) -- Fixes should not severely hamper the card's power. Some suggested
fixes tend to turn a card into wallpaper, in which case one it would be
simpler to say "This card is banned". There are other reasons for
preferring mild fixes. One is that the problem with fixes is getting a
consensus. A mild fix is more likely to gain the acquiescence of players
who just mailed away $30.00 for two copies of RTI. Another advantage of
mild fixes is that one can play them as house rules without too severely
altering the metagame. One is still forced to find a way to deal with
these powerful cards, and are not completely helpless when you encounter
them in tournament play. A final reason for mild fixes is that they are
more likely to gain the acquiescence of WOTC as far as making them
official. Like it or not, the overpowered nature of these cards has
created a demand for them, from which WOTC may have reaped some profit.

Lupus Australis

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Lupus Australius wrote:
"Day Operation Allies may still block"

This is good. Would make allies more useful. Day Opps isn't all _that_ bad,
however, unless it is used for RTI...

"Zip Gun Cannot use ammo"

Excellent.

"Tomb of Rameses III You may not transfer off the vampire with ToR"

Won't fix it that much, as you still can get out 2 IC members in 3 turns for 14
pool (and then Minion Tap them...). Our local group uses a very protracted fix
involving spending transfers to use the Tomb, but I am for simply banning it,
m'self.

"Pulled Fangs (etc.) Rule that it takes 2 ag to burn a vamp at 0 blood"

I prefer to give it the template used by Disarm (the obviosly fixed version of
PF included in Sabbat). Instead of doing aggro damage, PF should just say "Go
directly to torpor, do not pass go", just like Disarm. PF could not ever burn
a vamp in the original set, and it shouldn't be able to now.

"Thoughts Betrayed Not usable against older vamp"

Handy, but I still find the whole concept of the card offensive (i.e. not being
able to play the game). Our group uses it as "Opposing minion may not make any
strikes this round".

"Majesty (etc.)S:CE now means "S:Round Ends"- one may still press"

No need to fix. S:CE is an important defense, and there are enough perfectly
viable ways to screw with it as it is (Immortal Grapple, Psyche, Hidden Lurker,
Fast Reaction, Dawn Opps+DotB, the ever sketchy Dog Pack, the dispicable TB).
If you are building a deck that cares if its opponent plays S:CE, you can
easily prevent it (well, unless you are the Gangrel...). If your deck doesn't
care if they play S:CE, it just jams up their hand.

"Return to Innocence Requires vamp at capacity"

Completely unfixable. Requiring the vamp to be at full capacity is a bit of a
help, but that still means that the vamp who plays it will oust you in one
action. On any given turn I minion tap my IC member for 10, have someone else
play 5th Tradition on them, send them on RTI, play Dawn Opps, and kill you
unless you have a deflection in your hand, still. I think that RTI was a
misguided attempt to make it worth playing with big vampires, but all it
managed to do was screw up the play enviornment pretty severely.

Some cards we don't like around here are:

Banishment: Only useable on a younger vampire.

Mind Rape: Just wrong. We banned the sucker. In the original game design, it
was incredibly difficult to steal away someone elses vampire. You had a few
pool extensive master cards that were very iffy and required a bidding to
occur, Grave Robbing, which required the victim to be in torpor (and it wasn't
that easy for a deck with heavy DOM to put someone in torpor at that time), and
Malk Dementia, which is _highly_ situational. Mind Rape, however, is
completely free of conditionality and just too damn easy. It will be used to
steal a vamp and either RTI him or deablerize someone (or Golconda him or give
him up for the Antedeluvian Awakenings..). It was a mistake in the making.

Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
On 7 Mar 1998, PDB6 wrote:

> Lupus Australius wrote:
> "Day Operation Allies may still block"

> This is good. Would make allies more useful. Day Opps isn't all _that_
> bad, however, unless it is used for RTI...

I don't like "unblockability" in general. Too absolute. I would prefer
that blockability normally be expressed in terms of stealth and intercept.
An example might be:

Daylight Operations -- 1 blood -- fortitude - action modifier
Usable as the action is announced. Vampires without fortitude
have -6 intercept when attempting to block this action. The acting
vampire, and any vampire that attempts to block, will enter torpor when
the action resolves.
(S) As above, but vampires with inferior Fortitude have -3
intercept.

That's how I might have done it. It is, however, a new card design, and
not a fix.

> "Tomb of Rameses III You may not transfer off the vampire with ToR"

> Won't fix it that much, as you still can get out 2 IC members in 3 turns
> for 14 pool (and then Minion Tap them...). Our local group uses a very
> protracted fix involving spending transfers to use the Tomb, but I am
> for simply banning it, m'self.

You may be right. A fix I previously recommended was as follows:
Counters are placed on the Tomb, not the vampire. Each counts towards the
blood needed to enter play. [Needless to say, the counters are burned
with the Tomb, and the vampire comes out at less than full capacity.]
This may be too wordy, and perhaps violates my rule #1.

Lets see if I can express it in one line

Tomb of Rameses III Counters go on Tomb--each gives vamp -1 capacity

> "Pulled Fangs (etc.) Rule that it takes 2 ag to burn a vamp at 0 blood"

> I prefer to give it the template used by Disarm (the obviosly fixed
> version of PF included in Sabbat).

Are you advocating we ban it and use Disarm instead? Or that we use PF as
a proxy for Disarm?

> Instead of doing aggro damage, PF
> should just say "Go directly to torpor, do not pass go", just like
> Disarm. PF could not ever burn a vamp in the original set, and it
> shouldn't be able to now.

My fix causes it to work the same as in the original set, with the
difference that one loses a blood if one has it for the ag damage.

Under original ag rules, it took two ag to burn a vamp with 0 blood. My
fix will cause it to work exactly that way as far as burning is concerned.
It will also fix other agro cards like DBR, Sengir Dagger, Ivory Bow, Wolf
Claws, etc., making vampires far more difficult to burn and restoring
diablerie and the bloodhunt to their proper place in the game.

We need not return to the original ag rules, since they were judged too
confusing. Just rule that you need 2 more ag than a vampire has blood to
burn him.

I'm not sure if PF *could* burn a vampire under the original rules. If I
wolf claw and empty vamp for 1 damage, and then play PF as the round ends,
would this burn him? If I played 2 PF on an empty vamp would this burn
him? LSJ? I guess it depends on how you time the resolution of the
various ag damage cards, but it should work the same with my fix.

> "Thoughts Betrayed Not usable against older vamp"

> Handy, but I still find the whole concept of the card offensive (i.e.
> not being able to play the game). Our group uses it as "Opposing minion
> may not make any strikes this round".

Again, I would have designed a different card. Something like: "Name any
card--opposing minion may not play that card in the resulting combat. (S)
As above, but name any two cards." Idea is to punish opponent for
predictability. But that is of course, a totally different card design,
and not a fix.

I would suggest that, yours, while short and simple, is not a fix either.
The concept is completely different. The official TB allows strikes, but
forbids cards. Yours does the reverse (allows cards, but forbids
strikes). It's not so much a fix as it is a different card. You might as
well ban it if you're going to mess with it that much... or design your
own card and use "Concealed Weapon" as a proxy.

> "Majesty (etc.)S:CE now means "S:Round Ends"- one may still press"

> No need to fix. S:CE is an important defense, and there are enough
> perfectly viable ways to screw with it as it is (Immortal Grapple,
> Psyche, Hidden Lurker, Fast Reaction, Dawn Opps+DotB, the ever sketchy
> Dog Pack, the dispicable TB). If you are building a deck that cares if
> its opponent plays S:CE, you can easily prevent it (well, unless you are
> the Gangrel...). If your deck doesn't care if they play S:CE, it just
> jams up their hand.

I expected an argument on this one. S:CE is now such an accepted part
of the game that it's extremely profound effects on the game environment
are now accepted as natural. One of these effects was to turn (almost)
all press cards into wallpaper. Another was to make combat unfeasable for
those without multiple copies of a handful of uncommons and rares.

Even if S:CE only ended the round, it would still a far superior to other
combat defenses like Dodge. Dodge only prevents damage from one strike,
whereas S:CE also prevents additional strikes, retainer damage, and almost
all damage that can be inflicted on a vampire in combat. The only
advantage to a Dodge is that the dodger has the option of playing
additional strikes if he wishes, or still damaging opponent with own
retainers and environmental effects, etc.

The two cards should not have been so enormously different in power. Both
require discipines and usually cost 0 blood to play. There is, I admit, a
disciplineless version of "dodge", but it has a built-in disadvantage (do
not replace after combat) to make up for the lack of a discipline.

> "Return to Innocence Requires vamp at capacity"

> Completely unfixable. Requiring the vamp to be at full capacity is a
> bit of a help, but that still means that the vamp who plays it will oust
> you in one action. On any given turn I minion tap my IC member for 10,
> have someone else play 5th Tradition on them, send them on RTI, play
> Dawn Opps, and kill you unless you have a deflection in your hand,
> still. I think that RTI was a misguided attempt to make it worth
> playing with big vampires, but all it managed to do was screw up the
> play enviornment pretty severely.

I tend to agree that the card is wack. It is broken in combination with
so many other cards, such as Day Op, Temptation, Mind Rape, etc. I
certainly would not miss it if it were banned. Still this fix does cause
the person playing it a little more trouble. If your opponent keeps doing
mean things to you, even something as simple as Cryptic Mission, it can be
hard to play RTI. Doing RTI with Tempted, Mind-Raped, or Malk-Demented
vampires becomes more problematic when one must make sure they are at full
capacity first.

I should mention, though, that I once stealth-bled for 10 without RTI.
Queen Anne was the culprit. If I'd had Command of the Beast, I could
have done 11.

> Some cards we don't like around here are:
>
> Banishment: Only useable on a younger vampire.

Has it actually been a problem in your playgroup, or is it just the
concept you don't like.

> Mind Rape: Just wrong. We banned the sucker. In the original game
> design, it was incredibly difficult to steal away someone elses vampire.
> You had a few pool extensive master cards that were very iffy and
> required a bidding to occur, Grave Robbing, which required the victim to
> be in torpor (and it wasn't that easy for a deck with heavy DOM to put
> someone in torpor at that time), and Malk Dementia, which is _highly_
> situational. Mind Rape, however, is completely free of conditionality
> and just too damn easy. It will be used to steal a vamp and either RTI
> him or deablerize someone (or Golconda him or give him up for the
> Antedeluvian Awakenings..). It was a mistake in the making.

Hmmm. I do see the vampire-burning combo's as problematic, but otherwise
the card does would seem so overpowered to me. Let me make a few points.

- You only get to take one or possibly two actions with this vamp, and
only one master phase to do things to him.

- If the vamp is tapped when you take control of him, then you can take
only one action before returning him. If he is untapped, then he can
block you, and your action is not at stealth.

- You cannot use Dominate-based stealth, like bonding, because this is not
a bleed.

- I agree that Mind Rape has advantages over Grave Robbing. But Grave
Robbing effects older vampires, costs 0 blood, and gets you the vampire
permanently -- and the vampire you are trying to steal cannot block you.
Compare also to Far Mastery. It only costs 1 blood, is at +1 stealth, and
has the potential to get you a valuable minion -- permanently.

- The Golconda combo is problematic. To Mind Rape a vamp with capacity 8,
you need a vampire with capacity 9 or more -- and how will you know that
your opponent will be playing 8 capacity vampires? Then you have to make
sure the Golconda is in your hand next master phase.

- For the RTI combo, blame RTI, not Mind Rape. Either ban RTI or use my
fix, which should make playing it with stolen vampires slightly more
problematic. You might have to play Gird Minions on him first, or restore
him with 5th tradition.

I hadn't thought of the Antidiluvian Awakening combo. I agree
that something needs to be done about this. The intent of the card --
allowing one to use another Methuselah's vampire temporarily -- should
remain while its potential for abuse by destroying vampires permanently
should be minimized or eliminated. The easiest way to destroy a stolen
vampire, or indeed, any vampire, should be self-torporizing followed by
diablerie, risking the bloodhunt vote as usual.
Cards that burn vampires, even one's own vampires, are
problematic. I would rather see cards that burn vampires banned or
modified than Malk Dem, Temptation, or Mind Rape, since I feel the former
add rather less to the game atmosphere.

What really slows down combat decks is all the effort they have to put
into dealing with S:CE. I tried to address that below.

Diablerie and the risk of the bloodhunt vote were intended to be important
parts of the game. Burning a vamp without this risk was unlikely or very
costly. "Vulnerability" cost a master phase action and 2 pool.

With the new Agro damage rules, cards like Amaranth have become wallpaper.

ZipGun/DBR, will do the trick with such ease?

Note the "etc.". What do you think it refers to? I had in mind a
revision of the concept of S:CE that would effect all S:CE cards. In the
resulting card environment, presses would cease to be wallpaper. In a
heavy press environment, weapons would cease to be wallpaper, as their
benefits could be applied multiple times per combat. Cards only usable in
the second round would cease to be wallpaper. Ranged damage decks might
become feasible, through not having to rely on IG. Tremere would not need
disgusting cards like TB to have a chance in combat.

> but always over-looked. Any serious combat deck can whoop a S:CE deck.

I thought you just complained that combat was underpowered, in protest of
my suggested revision to agro damage rules.

> My gangrel deck relies on S:CE to kill vampires. That's also why they
> made Thoughts Betrayed. i do like the idea of S:Round ends though.
> Maybe in a future expansion, if that ever happens.

Perhaps, but that won't fix the excessive effect on the game environment
that S:CE already has.

> Return to Innocence Requires vamp at capacity
>

> I don't think this is neccesary at all, (see other post for reasoning),
> but instead try bleed at pluse x where x is amount of blood on vampire.
> Similar idea to yours, but not as limiting.

This does not interfere at all with broken RTI combos such as
MindRape/RTI, Temptation/RTI, or MalkDementia/RTI. Even mine may not
intefere with it enough, but it at least requires you go to the trouble of
making sure your temporarily stolen vampires are at full capacity. I would
rather place the blame on RTI than the latter cards, which I feel add more
to the game atmosphere. I am more of Peter's opinion that it might be
better to ban the card. It is involved in too many broken combos
(DayOp/RTI).

I should note that a full capacity requirement would only applies when you
play the card. You could still add Conditioning and Horrific Countenance
/Day Operation, and the action would still resolve normally. Perhaps I
should change it to "Cost x, where x is vampires capacity." That way, the
card would fizzle if you played any modifiers that cost blood.

however. Perhaps t'would be better to ban it.

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
(this is part one of an immense response)
Lupus Australius wrote:

(Dawn Opps)

"I don't like "unblockability" in general. Too absolute. I would prefer that
blockability normally be expressed in terms of stealth and intercept."

A fine point that I pretty much agree with. The card design you proposed is a
good one, if a bit wordy.

(Tomb)

"You may be right. A fix I previously recommended was as follows:
Counters are placed on the Tomb, not the vampire. Each counts towards the
blood needed to enter play. [Needless to say, the counters are burned with the
Tomb, and the vampire comes out at less than full capacity.] This may be too
wordy, and perhaps violates my rule #1."

The biggest problem I see with the Tomb as a card is that it is insanely
powerful, yet has _zero_ risk or disadvantage in its use. You play it and
immediately get back the 3 pool you spent on it, plus a profit of one pool, and
4 free transfers. If it survives another turn, you get even more. I always
was an advocate of some sort of mechanic that made it not work the turn it
comes out (maybe needing it to be tapped?), so there is a turn where it could
be blown up or stolen before it pays for itself. As it is, unless someone
Sudden Reversals it (and then you aren't required to pay for it anyway), it
always pays for itself and gives a definite bonus, even if it is killed on your
preys turn (the one pool and the 4 transfers).

(Pulled Fangs)

"Are you advocating we ban it and use Disarm instead? Or that we use PF as a
proxy for Disarm?"

No, I am advocating that the line on PF that says "Pulled Fangs inflicts 1
aggrivated damage," be replaced with the line "Put this card on the opposing
vampire and send that vampire into torpor.", just like on Disarm. The two
cards have different effects, and PF is disciplineless, so anyone can use it.
I just think it should not do aggrivated damage, just like Disarm.

"My fix causes it to work the same as in the original set, with the
difference that one loses a blood if one has it for the ag damage."

But then you are screwing with the rules of the game rather than the wording on
a single card. A bit stickier. For whatever reason, the designers thought
that the original aggro rules were too difficult to understand, so they changed
them. Sadly, PF became broken as a result. Just changing the wording on PF to
reflect the wording on Disarm fixes the problem.

"It will also fix other agro cards like DBR, Sengir Dagger, Ivory Bow, Wolf
Claws, etc., making vampires far more difficult to burn and restoring diablerie
and the bloodhunt to their proper place in the game."

The aggro rules aren't that bad in general (IMO), as it is real difficult to
land a burning aggro strke on someone with hand strikes and weapons. PF, on
the other hand, is incredibly potent (ahem...) when used by a Potence deck that
IGs you, hits you for 5 sending you to torpor anyway, and then plays PF,
burning you.

"We need not return to the original ag rules, since they were judged too
confusing. Just rule that you need 2 more ag than a vampire has blood to burn
him."

That is just as confusing (or not confusing as the case may be) as the original
rules were.

"I'm not sure if PF *could* burn a vampire under the original rules."

Nope. In each application of Aggro damage, the first point did no actual
damage, it just sent you to torpor.

(Thoughts Betrayed)

"I would suggest that, yours, while short and simple, is not a fix either."

Completely true. I don't think there really is a good way to fix the card and
leave it useful, while keeping it from being broken. The very concept--not
being able to play _any_ cards, the basic resource of the game--is faulty.
They could have designed any number of cards that had a combat effect similar
to TB but using a different mechanic, but they didn't. Your redesign (the pick
a card version) is a good one.

>But then you are screwing with the rules of the game rather than the wording on
>a single card. A bit stickier. For whatever reason, the designers thought
>that the original aggro rules were too difficult to understand, so they changed
>them. Sadly, PF became broken as a result. Just changing the wording on PF to
>reflect the wording on Disarm fixes the problem.

I personally think that the old aggro rules made a lot more sense.
You just need to look at what's actually considered to be happening,
rather than the numbers involved.

Here's my take on it, and how the original aggro rules make sense:

Each point of damage is powerful enough to send any vampire to torpor.
Each point of blood is enough to heal any vampire to full health.

But, you can't use blood to heal aggro damage, unless you're already
in torpor (if the RPG was followed more closely you couldn't use it
even when in torpor, but aggro is powerful enough already).

So if you take one point of damage, you need one blood to fix yourself
again so you don't go to torpor. If you take one point of damage that
you can't heal, you go to torpor. One way that happens is if you're
out of blood. The other way is if it's aggro.

If you have blood and take one aggro, you can't heal it so you go to
torpor anyway. no blood spent because you didn't fix anything.

Essentially what the new rules do is turn the first point of aggro you
deal into 2 points of aggro. one to send you to torpor and another to
damage you in torpor and make you spend a blood.

When explained properly I think the old rules make a lot more sense
than the new ones, and I think they're better for game balance as
well. Too bad a lot of people apparently couldn't get it.

Incidentally, though, if you follow this logic, PF could still be used
to burn a vampire. If it's used against a torporized vampire with
zero blood, the aggro can destroy the vampire and the vamp doesn't
have enough to heal it. It could not, however, be used to burn a vamp
with zero blood that was not in torpor.

-Dave Gausebeck

It may work as follows (old rules). You have 0 blood.

1 - I strike you with wolf claws for 1 agro. Damage resolves. You go
into torpor with 0 blood.
2 - At the end of the round, as you go into torpor, I play pulled fangs.

ruling that burning requires 2 points of agro in excess of current blood.

diablerie. Diablerie was also encouraged by the fact that it was so hard

did it "accidentally" in a fight. It has become a little too easy to
casually burn supposedly immortal vampires in the course of combat. I'm
not so much arguing that it unbalances the game as that it interferes with

enemies in combat should put Amaranth in their decks, and be prepared to

The way the original rulebook presents it, it's pretty ambiguous. It
says that the first point of aggro sends a vampire into torpor, but it
doesn't mention the case where the vampire is already in torpor. It
makes sense to me that aggro dealt to a vamp already in torpor would
be like excess aggro--it causes you to spend blood for healing
immediately or be burned if you can't. I believe that it was ruled
the other way, that it just sends you to torpor redundantly. I'm just
saying that my reasoning would give different results.

Lemme see if I can restate my idea on how I think damage makes the
most sense:

Each vampire has 3 states: ready, torpor, burned.

1 point of regular damage: if unhealed, sends a vampire from
ready->torpor. Does nothing to a vamp in torpor
1 point of aggro damage: if unhealed, sends a vampire from
ready->torpor OR torpor->burned

ready vampire: can spend 1 blood to heal 1 point of normal damage
vamp in torpor: can spend 1 blood to heal 1 point of aggro damage

you must spend blood to heal wounds if you can.

During strike resolution, deal with each point of unprevented damage
sequentially, normal first and then aggro.

If they had just put that in the original rulebook, along with a few
examples, I think there wouldn't have been any problems. Of course it
still lets you burn people with PF :P

game playable in a vaccum. You can show up at a table with a bunch of people
you don't know, will never see again, and play a cool game. That is one of the
main selling points of CCGs as a whole. In such a situation, you cannot rely
on a group effort or peer pressure to balance out broken cards.

In freindly play, while some people may enjoy screwing up the standard game
dynamic to deal with decks that rely on broken cards (like all 4 players in a
game ganging up on the 5th), others do not. When this is required to balance
out problems in the game, it is not an option. With broken cards removed from
the game (or fixed), and problems with the rules fixed up (like the DCI tourney
rules, for instance), this is no longer needed as a balance factor (but if you
still wanna do it, you can go to town...).

"It then becomes in THEIR interest to lose for a bit, eg by toning
down/changing their deck. This is what I understand by the Meta-game - doesn't
this happen anywhere else?"

It is never in anyones intrest to start losing. If someone feels they need to
stop winning so often because they are being constantly ganged up on by
everyone in the game, it seems likely that there is something wrong with the
play environment.

The "Meta-Game" is not about conspiring to beat up the guy who wins all the
time. The "Meta-Game" is about evolving deck strategies in a particular game
environment. For instance, around here, combat decks were all the rage for a
while. Any deck that wasn't able to deal with very brutal combat was just
destroyed, until people started showing up with decks that packed multiple Skin
of Steel and Obediance. These decks started winning alot, so the combat decks
fell out of favor. As a result, all the anti-combat cards that were so useful
before just started to clog up hands, and thus were removed from decks, because
no one was playing combat decks anymore, until someone realized that no one was
playing combat defense anymore, and so on. That is what makes the "Meta-Game"
good--evolving concepts and ideas. When the "Meta-Game" revolves around
everyone beating up the guy who is abusing a loophole or broken card, the game
becomes lame.

"Magic, where only two people ever play seriously, is different - there I
completely understand why cards have to be banned or their numbers limited. But
for heaven's sake let's not import Magic ways into our game!"

I fail to see the difference. In Magic, Lightning Bolt (or Hymn or Mind Twist
or the Moxen...) was determined to be broken--too good for what it cost.
Having 4 of them in your deck didn't automaticaly make you win, but the card
did have a greater effect on the game enviornment than was warranted. Thus, the
card was removed from the set. Why should the same thing not be done for
Jyhad, where certain cards have a far greater effect on the enviornemnt than
they should? The Tomb and RTI have a very profound effect on the game, because
they are just wrong. Cards like TB, Mind Rape, and Banishment have a far less
profound effect on the game, but still have an effect that is outweighed by
their cost, and consequently should be fixed in some way.

existance is justified. RTI, for example, is awfully close in effect to the

became very easy to bleed someone for 10+ pool in one action, with no warning
or preparation, and no disciplines. This has a very profound effect on the
game, because now, out of nowhere, you can be ousted by a single vampire with
no warning when you are at 15 pool. RTI has a cost, sure, but it is simply
not enough to balance it out. As a result, _all_ decks need to either play
Bleed Bounce, Archon Investigation, or Direct Intervention, otherwise
Unblockable RTI decks would become far and away the most dominanant decks in
the game. Before RTI, no deck was required to use any particular card. Now,
if you are not able to deal with unblockable RTI, you will be killed. This is
bad.

Daniel Freey wrote:
"But can we accept that Dog Pack and other cards have been reactively included

Yup. Adding a specific single card to a set to combat an entire strategy
simply does not work real well. Yes, Dog Pack, Atonement, and AI were added as
after the fact "patch" fixes to perceived game problems, but while they are
something of a fix on a small scale tactical level, in the strategic sense of
the game, there really aren't all that effective.

Dog Pack was added because the Gangrel are completley screwed by S:CE, and
helps a bit. However, retainers are not that effective on the whole due to
their lack of speed and fragility, Dog Pack is very expensive (2 Pool), and the
fact that it was rare certainly didn't help. In the log run, occasionally a
Gangrel deck will benefit from a Dog Pack but The Gangrel are still screwed on
the whole by S:CE, cause it is perfectly viable and acceptable to build a deck
with 10 Majesties in it, but a deck with 10 Dog Packs will suck a great deal of
the time.

Atonement is probably the most sucessful of the "patch" fixers, but still is
sketchy. A Weenie Horde Bleed deck will always work, but Atonement will only
work if it is next to a weenie horde bleed deck, otherwise it will mostly be
wasted cardage. I can build a WHB deck with 15 Social Charms, they will always
be useful. If I build an intercept deck with even half as many Atonements,
most of the time they will be little more than wasted cards.

Archon Investigation is very faulty in it's supposed original mission--stopping
S+B decks--as a competent S+B deck can easily kill you by consistently bleeding
you for 3 points an action leaving all your AIs completely wasted. As AI is a
master, you can really only have a few in your deck, making it highly unlikely
that you will actually have them when you need them (Having even 4 or 5 AIs in
your deck is bound to cause severe hand jam in the face of a non heavy bleed
deck, and having less of them means you can't rely on them as viable defense).
As a result, more often than not, AI is a lucky "Screw You" (or crap shooty)
card, but not a strategic defense.
